Don't ever insult the trilogy, and no even the ending of Mass Effect 3 didn't make "the world fall apart" (plus its more like a universe hue hue)

It was an interesting read and, mercifully, well written, but I don't fully agree. I've played both ME1 and ME2 to completion (wound up playing ME1 after ME2) and I've got ME3 sitting on my hard drive waiting to be played someday soon.

I found the parallel with LoTR interesting, though not entirely relevant. In the article, he points out what it would be like if Fellowship of the Ring had be written as it was, but Two Towers was handed off to a new author who decided to change the approach the heroes would use. Instead of rejecting the power of the ring and attempting to destroy it, a new wizard would appear and explain that Gandalf was wrong, a virtuous person could safely harness the power of the ring, and Frodo must now journey about and win over a vast army to confront Sauron. And that transition...from "it can't be controlled and must be destroyed" to "you can control it for the greater good" is the bad part. The reversal of sorts that trivializes the first book in the series. Can't do that. It's bad. Tolkien would never do that because he was too good of an author.

A more apt parallel, however, would be the one where Frodo and Sam head off to begin assembling their army and all of a sudden a Balrog appears, eats their ponies, and leaves them dangling by their ankles from the branches of a drunk Ent. So much for harnessing the power of the ring...

I know of another author who has risen to extraordinary fame and prominence specifically for slapping you in the head violently in the instant you think you know how things are going to proceed. His name is George R. R. Martin and of all the things he does well, killing pivotal characters just when they seem indispensable is something he's refining to a high art. Is it bad for a story when the author routinely flips it on its ear? Millions upon millions of Game of Thrones fans would seem to disagree. If anything, the only differentiating element Game of Thrones has that, for example, ME1 and ME2 do not, is that sudden massive power shifts and turns of fate are so common as to be an integral part of the story are become expected after a while (even though it always seems unexpected when they happen.)

So ME1 tells a story with an ending that leaves it wide open for a sequel, but could also tied off enough loose ends that the franchise could have been abandoned for many years and people wouldn't feel like they were missing an adequate resolution. It ends off basically sending Shepard and the crew of the Normandy off to explore and learn and discover more about this ominous threat. They've got the team, they've got the tech, they've got the balls. Get out there and explore!

And then at the beginning of ME2 the Reapers are all like, "NOPE!! Ain't got no time for fru-fru explorers! Fight bitches!"

Plans had to change. Rob Stark had the army, the resolve, and popular support to challenge the Lannisters for the Iron Throne at King's Landing. He even had a cool wife with an heir on the way.

Ooops. Plans had to change.

People who let these kinds of story changes bother them are basically getting mad that the author didn't write it the way they would have. That's all it is. Creative license being what it is, the pen is mightier than the assembled throng of livid fanboys and girls. If I have a story to tell I'll tell it. If someone else is telling the story, it's theirs to tell.
